input: The performance of a natural-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was monitored over the course of one summer month, and the principal results are summarised below. Natural-draft towers rely on the buoyancy of heated air rather than on fan power in order to draw the cooling air through the fill, and their performance is accordingly sensitive to the ambient conditions under which they operate. The logging exercise was undertaken in order to establish a baseline for the unit under normal summer operation, against which any future deterioration in performance might subsequently be assessed. Daily readings were gathered over the month as a whole and the values reported are the averages for the period, individual excursions on particular days having been absorbed into the monthly means. Over the period in question, the mean wet-bulb temperature was 24 °C, the approach was 4 K, and the range was 7 K. The approach represents the difference between the temperature of the cooled water leaving the tower and the wet-bulb temperature of the incoming air, from which it follows that the cold water left at approximately 28 °C, while the range, which represents the temperature fall of the water across the tower, implies a hot-water inlet temperature of some 35 °C. These results provide a useful indication of the tower's behaviour under the conditions that prevailed during the logging period, although it should be emphasised that performance outside the logged month was not measured. In particular, no data are available for winter wet-bulb temperatures, and the figures should therefore not be extrapolated to the colder part of the year without further supporting measurements being obtained.
target: Performance of a natural-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. The mean wet-bulb temperature over the month was 24 °C, the approach was 4 K and the range was 7 K. The approach is the difference between the cold-water temperature and the wet-bulb temperature, so the cold water left the tower at 28 °C; the range is the fall in water temperature across the tower, so the hot water entered at 35 °C. The three figures describe the tower as it ran in the logged month: the wet-bulb temperature is set by the weather and not by the tower, while the approach measures how closely the tower brought the cold water to that limit, and the range measures the heat taken out of each pass of the circulating water. A natural-draft tower has no fan, and its air flow is set by the density difference between the air inside the tower and the air outside it; the logged performance therefore belongs to the air temperatures and water loadings of the month in which it was recorded, and it does not transfer unchanged to other seasons. The record is a monthly mean in each case, and day-to-day variation within the month is not reported; a hot spell inside the month and a cool spell are averaged together in the figures as stated. The figures are also a statement about the circulating-water rate and the heat load of the month: the range is the joint outcome of the two, and the same tower on a different load would show a different range at the same wet-bulb temperature. Performance outside the logged month was not measured. Winter wet-bulb temperatures in particular lie outside the record, and the tower's behaviour at them — the approach it would hold and the range it would sustain — is not established by these figures.
